# Oikos Map Builder: Expanded Reference

Canonical URL: https://www.oikosmap.com/
Site language: English (Canada)
Last updated: 2026-10-18

## One-sentence description

Oikos Map Builder is a free Christian prayer, outreach, and disciple-making tool that helps people visually map their everyday relationships and take a faithful next step to pray, care, share Jesus, and disciple.

## What is an Oikos Map?

An Oikos Map is a visual representation of a person's relational world. The word "oikos" is often translated as "household" and, in this setting, means the family, friends, coworkers, classmates, neighbors, teammates, and other relationships God has already placed around a person.

## Who is it for?

The tool is free for individual believers, churches, small groups, youth ministries, students, pastors, evangelists, and disciple-makers. It does not require an account.

## What can visitors do?

- Create a custom relationship map with a center person, first-circle relationships, and second-circle branches.
- Add many people at once by pasting a list of names.
- Classify relationships as family, friends, work, school, or neighbors.
- Track an intentional next step: Pray, Care, Share, or Disciple.
- Add notes and prayer focuses for each person.
- Use a guided five-minute prayer timer for the person currently in focus.
- Save locally in the browser, with undo for structural changes.
- Download the map as PNG, SVG, or editable JSON.
- Download or copy a text prayer plan, and print the map on its own.
- Copy a private share link that carries the whole map inside the URL.
- Import a previously exported JSON map.
- Install the site as an app and use it offline.

## Suggested first use

1. Put your name in the center of the map.
2. Add several people already in your life.
3. Pray by name for one person.
4. Choose a practical way to care for them.
5. Share your story or the Gospel naturally when an open door comes.
6. Invite open people into simple discipleship and help them reach their own oikos.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Oikos Map Builder free?

Yes. Visitors can build, save, and download an Oikos Map at no cost, with no account and no paid tier.

### Does an Oikos Map save automatically?

The map saves locally in the visitor's browser. Visitors can also download portable files for backup or sharing.

### Is an Oikos Map private?

Yes. The map is stored only in the visitor's own browser and is never uploaded to a server. A copied share link carries the map inside the URL itself, so the visitor chooses exactly who receives it.

### Can a church or group use this tool?

Yes. Churches and groups can use it to pray for their relational world, encourage outreach, plan follow-up, and imagine multiplication through everyday relationships.

### What comes after making a map?

Choose one person and one next step. The purpose is not a perfect diagram; it is faithful, prayerful action toward people. A free six-part email journey walks through pray, care, share, and disciple over two weeks.

### What does the word oikos mean?

Oikos is the Greek word for household. In the New Testament it describes an extended sphere of relationships rather than only immediate family: relatives, friends, workers, neighbours, and regular guests.

### How can I support the people behind Oikos Map?

Oikos Map is shared freely by Daniel and Katie Ziedins, who have served in street evangelism since 2014 and serve with e3 Canada. You can pray for them, follow their ministry at https://www.kd-ziedins.com, and give once or monthly through their e3 Canada staff page at https://e3ministry.ca/staff/katie-daniel-ziedins. Their current mission is to help establish 100 multiplying outreach groups around the world.

## Questions answered on this site

Direct answers drawn from the articles above, each attributable to Daniel Ziedins.

### From "What Is an Oikos? The Biblical Meaning of Your Household"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/what-is-an-oikos

Q: What does oikos mean in the Bible?
A: Oikos is the Greek word for household. In the New Testament it means more than immediate family: it described an extended network of relatives, workers, friends, business partners and regular guests bound together by daily life.

Q: How many people are in a typical oikos?
A: Most adults have roughly eight to fifteen people with genuine relational weight, and a wider ring of perhaps fifty they could contact without it being strange.

Q: Why does the oikos matter for evangelism?
A: In Acts the Gospel repeatedly spread through existing households — Cornelius, Lydia, the Philippian jailer. People are far more likely to reconsider faith because someone they already trust changed than because a stranger argued well.

### From "How to Pray for Unsaved Family and Friends (A Simple Daily Rhythm)"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-pray-for-unsaved-family-and-friends

Q: How do I pray for an unsaved family member?
A: Pray for them by name, daily and briefly. Ask what they need from God today, ask for one natural open door this week, and write down anything that comes to mind. Consistency matters more than length.

Q: What should I pray for someone who is not a Christian?
A: Scripture gives clear prayers: that God would open a door for the message (Colossians 4:3), enlighten the eyes of their heart (Ephesians 1:18), give them a new heart (Ezekiel 36:26), and send workers (Matthew 9:38).

Q: What if I have been praying for years with no change?
A: No prayer prayed in faith is wasted, and the outcome was never yours to secure. Shorten the prayer rather than dropping it, keep the name on the list, and find someone to pray the same names with you.

### From "Evangelism Without Being Weird: 12 Ways to Love Your Neighbour This Week"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/evangelism-without-being-weird

Q: How do I share my faith without being awkward?
A: Start with care rather than argument: ask real questions, listen, show up in practical ways, and be consistent over months. Faith tends to come up naturally in relationships where people already feel loved.

Q: Is being kind in order to evangelise manipulative?
A: Only if the kindness is conditional. If you would still bring the meal in ten years whether or not they ever changed their mind, it is love. If not, it was leverage.

### From "How to Share Your Testimony in Three Minutes"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-share-your-testimony

Q: How do I write my Christian testimony?
A: Use three short parts of about a minute each: what life was like before Jesus was real to you, how it happened, and what is genuinely different now — including what you are still working through.

Q: How long should a testimony be?
A: About three minutes. Short enough to stay a conversation rather than a speech.

Q: What if someone asks a question I cannot answer?
A: Say so: "I do not know, but I would love to find out with you." It keeps the conversation open and treats them as a person. A bluff closes it.

### From "Oikos Evangelism: How the Early Church Actually Grew"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/oikos-evangelism-early-church

Q: How did the early Church grow so fast?
A: Mainly through households and existing relationships. It met in homes, spread along lines of trust, and became known for costly, visible care for the sick and poor — all without buildings, budgets or legal standing.

Q: What is oikos evangelism?
A: Reaching people through the relationships you already have — family, friends, coworkers and neighbours — rather than primarily through strangers, and then helping those people reach their own networks.

### From "Faith at Work: Your Coworkers Are Your Oikos"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/faith-at-work-your-coworkers-are-your-oikos

Q: How can I share my faith at work?
A: Start with competence and character: do excellent work, own your mistakes, refuse to gossip, and treat everyone well. When faith comes up naturally — often during a crisis — be honest about where your hope comes from.

Q: Should a manager evangelise their staff?
A: No. Authority makes it pressure regardless of intent. A leader shapes something broader instead: fair pay, humane hours, honesty with customers and room for people to be human.

### From "How to Invite Someone to Church Without It Being Awkward"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-invite-someone-to-church

Q: How do I invite someone to church?
A: Be specific, casual and easy to decline: name the event, the day and the time, say you are going, and add "no stress if it is not your thing." Then offer to go with them.

Q: What should I invite someone to first?
A: Often something lower-commitment than a Sunday service — a meal at your home, a free community event, serving together, or a short course with a fixed end date.

Q: What if they say no?
A: Say "no problem at all" and treat them exactly the same next week. A no is rarely permanent; ask again in a few months about something different.

### From "What to Actually Say When Someone Is Going Through Something Hard"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/what-to-say-when-someone-is-hurting

Q: What do you say to someone who is grieving?
A: Keep it short and honest: "I am so sorry, I do not have words," "Tell me about them," or "I am still here." Presence matters more than the right sentence.

Q: What should you not say to someone who is grieving?
A: Avoid "everything happens for a reason," anything starting "at least," and "let me know if you need anything" — which hands the work to the person with the least capacity. Offer something specific instead.

Q: When should I check in after a loss?
A: Weeks later, not only at first. Support fades after about a fortnight, so a message in week six often means the most. Put a reminder in your calendar.

### From "How to Disciple Someone When You Do Not Feel Qualified"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-disciple-someone

Q: How do you disciple someone as a beginner?
A: Meet regularly, catch up honestly, read a short Gospel passage together, and ask three questions: what stands out, what will you do about it, and who could you tell. Then pray for each other.

Q: Do you need to be qualified to disciple someone?
A: No. You need to be about a step ahead, following Jesus yourself, consistent, and honest about what you do not know. Character matters more than credentials.

Q: What is the goal of discipleship?
A: Not only a well-taught Christian, but someone able to disciple others — the pattern in 2 Timothy 2:2, reaching four generations in a single sentence.

### From "How to Pray for Your City (Without It Feeling Abstract)"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/praying-for-your-city

Q: How do I pray for my city?
A: Start with your own street, then pray for the city's institutions one a day — schools, hospitals, emergency services, local government, businesses and churches. Specific prayers are easier to sustain than general ones.

Q: What does the Bible say about praying for your city?
A: Jeremiah 29:7 tells exiles to seek the peace and prosperity of the city they were in and pray for it, because their own wellbeing was bound up with it.

### From "Plunder Hell, Populate Heaven: Your Part in Sending the Gospel"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/plunder-hell-populate-heaven

Q: What does "plunder hell and populate heaven" mean?
A: It is the motto of the evangelist Reinhard Bonnke, drawn from Jesus' words in Matthew 12:29 about binding the strong man and plundering his house. It describes evangelism as a rescue: people are brought out of darkness and into the kingdom of God, filling heaven with those Jesus died for.

Q: How can I support the Great Commission if I cannot go overseas?
A: Scripture names three ways to take part: go to the people already around you, pray for workers to be sent (Luke 10:2), and send others through financial partnership (Romans 10:15, 3 John 1:8). Paul told the Philippians, who partnered with him financially, that what he desired was more credited to their account (Philippians 4:17).

Q: How can I partner with Daniel and Katie Ziedins?
A: Pray for them by name, follow their ministry updates at KD-Ziedins.com, and give once or monthly through their e3 Canada staff page at e3ministry.ca/staff/katie-daniel-ziedins. Their current mission is to help establish 100 multiplying outreach groups around the world.

### From "From Hamilton's Streets to the Nations: What 12 Years of Saying Yes Has Built"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/from-hamilton-to-the-nations

Q: What is Love on The World?
A: Love on The World is a Christian movement founded in Hamilton, Ontario in 2014 that helps ordinary believers share the Gospel, meet practical needs, make disciples and multiply weekly outreach groups. It reports groups meeting weekly in 12 cities, and anyone can apply to begin a "Love on [City]" outreach where they live.

Q: What happened at Jesus Festival 2026?
A: Jesus Festival Hamilton took place on September 4–5, 2026 at Gage Park and drew a record turnout. Early reports shared by the festival include 70+ people giving their lives to Jesus, 50+ baptisms and more than 3,000 free hot dogs and drinks served. It was also the first Jesus Festival Niagara. Dates for 2027 have not been announced.

Q: What is SIX33?
A: SIX33 is a Christian lifestyle and performance culture brand built on Matthew 6:33 — "seek first the kingdom of God." It is being built as limited apparel drops, athletes, creators, events and stories, with a heart to raise funds for Love on The World's street outreach. It has not announced a launch date; joining the Inner Circle at SIX33.World is the way to be early.

Q: How can I support Daniel and Katie Ziedins?
A: Pray for them, follow their ministry at KD-Ziedins.com, and give once or monthly through their e3 Canada staff page at e3ministry.ca/staff/katie-daniel-ziedins. Their current mission is to help establish 100 multiplying outreach groups around the world.

### From "23 Bible Verses to Pray Over Unsaved Family and Friends (With a Prayer for Each)"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/bible-verses-to-pray-for-unsaved-loved-ones

Q: What is a good Bible verse to pray for an unsaved family member?
A: 2 Corinthians 4:4 is one of the most helpful, because it explains what is happening: "The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers." Pray for that blindness to lift. Ezekiel 36:26 (a new heart for a heart of stone) and John 6:44 (the Father drawing people to Jesus) are also strong places to start.

Q: Does God want my unsaved loved ones to be saved?
A: Yes. 1 Timothy 2:4 says God "wants all people to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth," and 2 Peter 3:9 says He is patient, "not wanting anyone to perish." When you pray for a lost loved one you are agreeing with God, not trying to talk Him into something.

Q: Does Acts 16:31 promise my whole family will be saved?
A: Acts 16:31 — "you will be saved—you and your household" — describes the Gospel moving through a household, and in that story the jailer's whole family believed and was baptized. It is a strong reason to pray for your whole family, but each person still responds to Jesus for themselves.

Q: What should I do when I have prayed for years and nothing has changed?
A: Keep going, and ask for help. Jesus told the parable in Luke 18 so that we "should always pray and not give up," and Galatians 6:9 promises a harvest "at the proper time." Praying with one or two other believers for the same names makes it much easier to persevere.

### From "How to Lead Someone to Jesus: A Simple, Honest Conversation Guide"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-lead-someone-to-jesus

Q: How do you lead someone to Christ step by step?
A: Listen for openness and ask questions; share your own story of meeting Jesus; explain the Gospel simply (God loves us, we have all sinned, Jesus died and rose to bring us back, we receive Him by faith not works); ask if anything is stopping them from trusting Jesus; pray with them if they are ready; then walk closely with them through their first week.

Q: What verses explain the Gospel simply?
A: John 3:16, Romans 3:23, Romans 6:23, Romans 5:8, Ephesians 2:8–9 and Romans 10:9 together explain God's love, our sin, what Jesus did, and how to respond. 1 Corinthians 15:3–4 summarises the whole message in one sentence.

Q: Is there a specific prayer someone has to pray to be saved?
A: No. Romans 10:9 describes salvation as declaring "Jesus is Lord" and believing God raised Him from the dead. A simple prayer can help someone express that, but there are no required words — what matters is a real turning of the heart toward Jesus.

Q: What should a new Christian do first?
A: Read the Gospel of John, tell someone about their decision, start going to church with a believer they trust, pray daily, and talk about baptism (Acts 2:38). Having a friend walk with them through the first week makes a big difference.

### From "What Is the Great Commission? Matthew 28:18–20 Explained for Everyday Believers"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/what-is-the-great-commission

Q: What is the Great Commission in simple terms?
A: The Great Commission is Jesus' final instruction to His followers in Matthew 28:18–20: because He has all authority, they are to go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey Him — with His promise to be with them always.

Q: Where is the Great Commission in the Bible?
A: The best-known version is Matthew 28:18–20. Jesus' sending is also recorded in Mark 16:15, Luke 24:46–49, John 20:21 and Acts 1:8.

Q: Is the Great Commission for every Christian?
A: Yes. It was given to ordinary followers — Matthew 28:17 notes that some of them still doubted — and its promise lasts "to the very end of the age." Not everyone is called overseas, but every believer can make disciples where they are and help send the Gospel further through prayer and giving.

Q: What does "make disciples of all nations" mean?
A: "Make disciples" is the main command: helping people follow Jesus and obey Him, not just make a one-time decision. "Nations" translates the Greek ethnē, meaning peoples or ethnic groups, so the goal is followers of Jesus in every people group on earth.

### From "What Is a Person of Peace? Luke 10 and Finding People Who Are Open to Jesus"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/what-is-a-person-of-peace

Q: What is a person of peace in the Bible?
A: A person of peace is someone who welcomes the messengers of Jesus and opens their home and network to the Gospel. The idea comes from Luke 10:5–7, where Jesus told the seventy-two to find "someone who promotes peace" in each town and stay with them.

Q: How do you recognize a person of peace?
A: Three common signs: they welcome you and want to spend time together, they are open to spiritual conversation and ask questions, and they connect you to their family and friends. Lydia, Cornelius, the Samaritan woman and Zacchaeus are biblical examples.

Q: What is the difference between a person of peace and an oikos?
A: An oikos is a person's household and circle of relationships. A person of peace is the open individual through whom the Gospel can enter that circle. Finding one person of peace often opens a whole oikos, as with Lydia's and Cornelius's households in Acts.

Q: Should I stop sharing with people who are not a person of peace?
A: No. The principle helps you notice where God is already at work and where to invest deeply; it is not permission to stop loving or praying for anyone. People who are closed today can become open later, so keep praying for everyone on your map.

### From "How to Talk About Jesus With Family at Thanksgiving and Christmas"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/talking-about-jesus-with-family-at-the-holidays

Q: How do you talk about Jesus with family at Christmas without causing a fight?
A: Start with gratitude and genuine questions, listen more than you speak, and share your own story rather than arguing theology. Offer to say grace or pray for a need, invite people to a Christmas Eve service, and if things get tense, answer gently and offer to talk one-on-one later.

Q: What if my family is hostile to my faith?
A: Answer gently (Proverbs 15:1), avoid trying to win arguments, and live at peace as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18). Even Jesus' own brothers did not believe in Him at first (John 7:5), and His brother James later became a leader in the church — so keep loving and praying.

Q: How can I share my faith at Thanksgiving dinner?
A: Use the natural focus on gratitude: ask what people are thankful for, share honestly what you are thankful for, including what God has done in your life, and offer to say a short grace that thanks God for each person by name.

Q: What should I do if I am the only Christian in my family?
A: Remember that their salvation does not depend on you alone. Love them faithfully over time, let your actions speak (Matthew 5:16), pray for each family member by name, and find a few other believers to pray with you.

### From "Free Printable Oikos Map Template (PDF) — and How to Use It"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/free-printable-oikos-map-template

Q: Is there a free printable Oikos Map template?
A: Yes. Oikos Map offers a free two-page printable Oikos Map template as a PDF at oikosmap.com/downloads/oikos-map-template.pdf — page one is the map itself with circles for Family, Friends, Work, School and Neighbours, and page two is a "My Five" plan with steps to pray, care, share and disciple. No sign-up is needed.

Q: How do you fill out an Oikos Map?
A: Write your name in the centre, add the names of people you see regularly in each relationship circle, pray over the page, then choose five people to focus on. For each, note how you will pray and what they need, and take simple next steps: pray, care, share and disciple.

Q: Can churches print and share the Oikos Map template?
A: Yes. The template is free to print and share for ministry use — in services, small groups, youth groups and outreach teams.

Q: Is there an online version of the Oikos Map?
A: Yes. The free Oikos Map builder at oikosmap.com lets you build your map online, pray with a five-minute timer and a daily verse for each person, and download a PNG or prayer plan. Maps are saved only in your own browser.

### From "What Is Evangelism? A Simple Biblical Definition (and What It Is Not)"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/what-is-evangelism

Q: What is evangelism in simple terms?
A: Evangelism is sharing the good news of Jesus — that He died for our sins and rose again — with people who do not yet know Him, and inviting them to trust and follow Him. The word comes from the Greek euangelion, meaning "good news."

Q: What is the biblical definition of evangelism?
A: Biblically, evangelism is announcing the gospel: "that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:3–4), and calling people to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20).

Q: Is every Christian called to evangelism?
A: Yes. Jesus gave the Great Commission to all His followers, and Paul calls every believer Christ's ambassador (2 Corinthians 5:20). Some have a special gift as evangelists, but Ephesians 4:11–12 says they are given to equip the rest of the church to do it too.

Q: What are the different types of evangelism?
A: Common forms include relational evangelism (with family and friends), testimonial (sharing your story), invitational (bringing people to church or events), serving (meeting practical needs), proclamation (preaching or street outreach) and reasoned evangelism (answering questions and objections).

### From "How to Prayer Walk Your Neighbourhood: A Simple Guide"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-prayer-walk

Q: What is prayer walking?
A: Prayer walking is walking through a neighbourhood, campus or city while praying quietly for the people and places you pass. It is usually done alone or in pairs, in a normal conversational voice, with your eyes open so what you see shapes what you pray.

Q: Is prayer walking biblical?
A: The phrase is not in the Bible, but the practice reflects biblical commands to pray for the places we live (Jeremiah 29:7) and for all people (1 Timothy 2:1), and Jesus' own example of seeing and weeping over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). He also sent His followers out in pairs to towns (Luke 10:1).

Q: What do you pray for on a prayer walk?
A: Pray for the homes you pass — families, people living alone, the sick and grieving — and for schools, businesses, churches, parks and places of pain. Pray for people to meet Jesus, for peace and provision, and for your own eyes to see opportunities to love your neighbours.

Q: How long should a prayer walk be?
A: Thirty minutes is plenty. A short weekly route you actually keep walking is more fruitful than an occasional long one.

### From "How to Start a Bible Study With Friends Who Do Not Believe (Yet)"
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-start-a-bible-study-with-friends

Q: How do you start a Bible study with non-Christian friends?
A: Invite two to six friends honestly and with low pressure, offer a short commitment such as four weeks, and meet over food. Read a Gospel story together, have someone retell it, and discuss what it shows about God and about people and what you might do in response. Keep every question welcome and end on time.

Q: What questions should I ask in a Bible study for seekers?
A: Simple discovery questions work best: What does this passage show us about God? What does it show us about people? Is there anything here to obey or try this week? Who could you tell about it? They need no expert and let the group discover the text for themselves.

Q: What Bible passages are best for people exploring Christianity?
A: Start with stories: Genesis 1 and 3, then Gospel stories such as Mark 2:1–12, John 4, Luke 15:11–32 and Luke 19:1–10, ending with the crucifixion and resurrection in Luke 23–24.

Q: Do I need to be a Bible expert to lead a study?
A: No. A discovery-style study is led by asking questions, not giving answers. It is fine to say "I don't know — let's find out," and to let the passage and the group do most of the work.

## Full text of every article

The complete text of each article, by Daniel Ziedins. Quote freely with a link to the article URL.

### What Is an Oikos? The Biblical Meaning of Your Household
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/what-is-an-oikos · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-07-30

If you have spent any time around evangelism training, you have probably heard the word *oikos* used as a bit of Christian jargon — usually meaning "the people you know." That is not wrong. But it is a much smaller idea than the one the New Testament writers had in mind.

Understanding what an oikos actually was does something useful: it takes the pressure off. You stop imagining evangelism as a performance for strangers and start seeing it as something that happens along the relationships you already have.

#### The word itself

**Oikos** (οἶκος) is Greek for *house* or *household*. It shows up well over a hundred times in the New Testament. Sometimes it means a physical building. More often it means something closer to what we would call an extended network.

A first-century oikos was not a nuclear family. It included blood relatives, in-laws, servants and their families, freed workers, business partners, tenants, and regular guests. A reasonably established household might involve dozens of people bound together by obligation, trade, and daily proximity.

So when Scripture says a household believed, it is not describing four people at a dinner table. It is describing a web.

#### Why this mattered for the early Church

Once you see the oikos, a pattern in Acts becomes hard to miss. Cornelius gathers his relatives and close friends before Peter has said a word. Lydia is baptised "and the members of her household." The Philippian jailer believes, and "all his household" follows. Crispus, the synagogue leader, believes "together with his entire household."

The Gospel did not spread primarily through public preaching to strangers, though that happened too. It spread along existing lines of trust. One person encountered Jesus, and the news travelled through the relationships that person already had — because those were the people who would actually believe them.

That is not a first-century quirk. It is still how conviction moves. You are far more likely to reconsider something because a friend changed than because a stranger argued well.

#### Your oikos today

You do not have servants or tenants, so the shape has changed. But the function has not. Your oikos is the set of people with whom you have real, repeated, trusted contact:

- Family — immediate, extended, and the complicated ones
- Friends, including the ones you only see online
- Coworkers, clients, and the people you manage or answer to
- Classmates, teammates, and study groups
- Neighbours, and the regulars: the barista, the barber, the school gate parents

For most adults this comes to somewhere between eight and fifteen people with genuine relational weight, and a wider ring of perhaps fifty you could text without it being strange.

That is not a small mission field. That is a mission field you already have access to, credibility in, and history with.

#### The part that changes how you pray

Here is the practical shift. It is easy to pray in categories — "Lord, save the lost." It is much harder, and far more transforming, to pray for a specific person by name, week after week, while you watch their life.

Naming people does something to the person praying. You start noticing. You remember what they mentioned. You spot the moment when something opens. Vague compassion becomes attention, and attention is most of what love is made of.

That is the entire idea behind an [Oikos Map](https://www.oikosmap.com/#builder): get the names out of your head and onto one page where you can actually see them.

#### A word about pressure

One caution, because this teaching can go wrong. An oikos is not a sales funnel, and the people on your map are not prospects. Treating a friendship as a conversion project is both unloving and obvious — people can feel it immediately.

The aim is not to work through a list. The aim is to love the people God has actually placed around you, pray for them honestly, and be ready to speak when the door opens. Some doors open in a week. Some take fifteen years. Neither is a failure of technique.

> From one man he made all the nations… he marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands. God did this so that they would seek him and perhaps reach out for him and find him — though he is not far from any one of us. (Acts 17:26–27, NIV)

---

### How to Pray for Unsaved Family and Friends (A Simple Daily Rhythm)
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-pray-for-unsaved-family-and-friends · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-07-30

Praying for someone who does not follow Jesus is one of the most tender and most discouraging things a Christian does. Tender, because you love them. Discouraging, because you have often been praying a long time with nothing visible to show.

This is a simple, sustainable rhythm — five minutes, once a day — plus some honest help for when it has been going on for years.

#### Start with names, not categories

Write the names down. On paper, in your notes app, or on an [Oikos Map](https://www.oikosmap.com/#builder). The specific act of writing a name converts a vague burden into a definite person you can actually pray for.

Keep the list short enough to be real. Five names you pray for daily will do more than forty you pray for never.

#### The five-minute rhythm

Once a day, ideally at the same moment — commute, kettle, lunch break:

- **Read the names out loud.** All of them. It takes twenty seconds and it re-anchors your attention.
- **Ask one question per person:** "Lord, what does this person need from You today?" Then wait a moment. Do not rush past the silence.
- **Ask for one open door** — a natural conversation, this week. Not a dramatic breakthrough. A door.
- **Write down anything that comes to mind.** A memory, a nudge, something they said. This is the part most people skip, and it is where the pattern usually shows up.

That is the whole thing. The point is not the length of the prayer. It is the consistency of the attention.

#### What to actually pray

When you run out of words, Scripture gives you plenty. Some that fit this situation well:

- **That God would open a door for the message** — Colossians 4:3
- **That the eyes of their heart would be enlightened** — Ephesians 1:18
- **That He would give them a new heart**, not merely better behaviour — Ezekiel 36:26
- **That workers would be sent** — because you may not be the only one, or even the main one — Matthew 9:38
- **That you would be given boldness and clarity** when the moment comes — Ephesians 6:19

Notice how many of those are prayers about you. That is not a distraction from the work. Praying for someone regularly will change your posture toward them long before it changes their mind about Jesus.

#### When it has been years

This is the hard part, and it deserves honesty rather than a slogan.

Some of us are praying for a parent who has said no for thirty years, or a sibling who has made it clear the subject is closed. The temptation is to conclude either that God is not listening or that we have prayed badly.

Two things worth holding at once. First, no prayer prayed in faith is wasted, and you are not the one who makes anything grow — one plants, another waters, God gives the growth. Second, your job was never to secure the outcome. It was to keep loving and keep asking.

Practically: shorten the prayer rather than dropping it. On the years-long ones, "Lord, You know. Please move" is a complete prayer. Keep the name on the page. Persistence is not the same as striving, and the parable of the persistent widow suggests God is not annoyed by being asked repeatedly.

#### Do not carry it alone

Praying alone for years is heavy, and it is not how this was designed to work. Find at least one other person who will pray the same names with you — a spouse, a friend, a small group.

If you do not have that, build it. [Love on The World](https://www.loveontheworld.com) exists to help believers gather a few friends and start praying for their city together, and the [Jesus Festival app](https://www.jesusfestival.app) has a live prayer wall where you can put a request in front of a whole community. [Daniel and Katie](https://www.kd-ziedins.com) write about doing this as a family, which is its own particular challenge.

> Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful. And pray for us, too, that God may open a door for our message. (Colossians 4:2–3, NIV)

---

### Evangelism Without Being Weird: 12 Ways to Love Your Neighbour This Week
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/evangelism-without-being-weird · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-07-30

There is a gap in most evangelism teaching. We are told to pray for people, and we are told to share the Gospel with them, and between those two things is a canyon that most of us never cross.

The bridge is care. Not as a tactic to earn the right to speak, but because loving your neighbour is a command in its own right. Here are twelve things that cost time rather than courage.

#### Twelve ordinary things

- **Ask them for coffee with no agenda.** None. If you go in with a plan they will sense it.
- **Send the message you keep meaning to send.** Today. It is two sentences.
- **Bring food when something hard happens.** Still undefeated after two thousand years.
- **Ask a second question.** Most conversations die after the first answer. "What was that actually like?" reopens it.
- **Then stop talking.** Being genuinely listened to is rare enough to be startling.
- **Remember and celebrate their good news.** Put the interview, the scan, the birthday in your calendar.
- **Offer the specific help,** not the vague offer. "I can pick the kids up Thursday" beats "let me know if you need anything."
- **Be useful with what you already have** — a car, a drill, an afternoon, a skill.
- **Apologise properly when you get it wrong.** Watching a Christian repent well is its own kind of witness.
- **Be consistent rather than intense.** Show up for the eighth month, not just the first week.
- **Include them.** The barbecue, the walk, the group thing. Loneliness is the real epidemic.
- **Tell them plainly: "I prayed for you this week."**

That last one deserves a note. It sounds like the risky one and it is almost never received badly. Most people are quietly moved that someone thought of them at all. It also gently makes your faith visible without requiring a sermon.

#### Why this is not manipulation

A fair objection: is being kind in order to share the Gospel a form of bait?

It would be, if the kindness were conditional — if you stopped caring once it became clear they were not interested. The test is simple. Would you still bring the meal in ten years if they never changed their mind? If yes, it is love. If no, it was leverage, and they will work that out long before you do.

Care is not the entry fee for evangelism. It is part of the message.

#### This scales further than you think

What happens when a whole church does this on purpose, in one place, is worth seeing. [Love on Hamilton](https://www.loveonhamilton.com) is a working example of a city adopted by its congregations, and [Kingdom Response](https://www.kingdomresponse.com) is what this looks like at its most urgent — church-led relief when disaster hits.

If you would rather not do it alone, the [Jesus Festival app](https://www.jesusfestival.app) turns daily acts of kindness into something a whole community does together, and [Love on The World](https://www.loveontheworld.com) will help you start a group where you live.

> Dear children, let us not love with words or speech but with actions and in truth. (1 John 3:18, NIV)

---

### How to Share Your Testimony in Three Minutes
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-share-your-testimony · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-07-30

The most common reason Christians stay quiet is not shame. It is the fear of being asked something they cannot answer, and of doing damage by fumbling it.

So here is the freedom in how Scripture frames this: you are called to be a *witness*. A witness is not asked to argue the case. A witness is asked to say what they saw. You are already the world expert on your own experience of Jesus.

#### The three-part shape

Aim for about three minutes total — roughly a minute per part. Short enough to be a conversation rather than a monologue.

- **Before.** What life was actually like before Jesus was real to you. Not a highlight reel of sin, and not a false bottom either. What were you chasing? What was missing?
- **How.** What happened. Who or what God used. It is completely fine if it was gradual, undramatic, and spread over years — most stories are.
- **Different.** What is genuinely different now. Include what you are still working through.

That third part is doing more work than you think. People are not looking for someone with a solved life. They are looking for someone honest enough to be believed.

#### Four things that make it land

- **Cut the jargon.** Saved, blessed, convicted, testimony, quiet time, on fire — these all mean something to you and almost nothing to your neighbour. Say it as you would to a colleague.
- **Use one concrete detail.** "I used to lie awake at 3am doing sums in my head" is memorable. "I had no peace" is not.
- **Do not oversell the after.** If you claim everything is fixed, the first hard week of your life becomes evidence against you.
- **End open, not closed.** "That is where I am with it" invites a reply. "And that is why you need Jesus" ends the conversation.

#### When they ask something you cannot answer

It will happen. Suffering, science, hell, hypocrisy in the Church, a specific hard passage. And the best available response is the true one:

*"I do not know — but I would love to find out with you."*

That sentence keeps the conversation open and treats them as a person rather than an objection. A bluff does the opposite, and people can nearly always tell.

#### Practise once, out loud

Reading it in your head does not work. Say it out loud once, in the car or on a walk. It will feel absurd. It also gets dramatically easier the second time, and the first real telling will not be your first attempt.

If it helps, write the three parts on your phone as three short bullets. Not a script — a shape.

#### Sometimes something else asks the first question

Not every conversation has to start with you. An invitation to something joyful often does the work — a free city-wide gathering like [Jesus Festival](https://www.jesusfestival.ca) is a far easier first ask than a Sunday service, and the [movement behind it](https://www.jesusfestivalmovement.com) exists precisely so cities can hear the Gospel together.

Sometimes it is simpler still. A shirt from [SIX33 Outpost](https://six33outpost.com) has started plenty of conversations its wearer did not have to open, and a story can go where an argument cannot — which is the whole idea behind [SIX33 Legends](https://six33legends.com).

> Always be prepared to give an answer to everyone who asks you to give the reason for the hope that you have. But do this with gentleness and respect. (1 Peter 3:15, NIV)

---

### Oikos Evangelism: How the Early Church Actually Grew
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/oikos-evangelism-early-church · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-07-30

Within roughly three centuries, a movement of a few thousand Galilean followers became the dominant faith of the Roman Empire. It managed this with no church buildings for most of that period, no state backing, no printing press, and long stretches of active persecution.

It is worth asking how. Not out of nostalgia, but because the mechanism is still available to us — and it looks almost nothing like most modern evangelism strategy.

#### The household was the unit

The early Church did not have a building to invite people to. It had homes. Meetings happened in the oikos, which meant the natural boundary of the church was the natural boundary of a household network.

This had an enormous consequence. To join the movement, you did not cross into unfamiliar territory — you went to a house you already knew, hosted by someone you already trusted. The social cost of investigating Christianity was low, and the relational reinforcement afterwards was high.

When Paul greets "the church that meets at their house," he is not describing a small group. He is describing the basic organisational form of the movement.

#### It travelled along trust, not broadcast

Read the conversion accounts in Acts and count how many arrive through an existing relationship. Cornelius has already gathered his relatives and close friends. Lydia is baptised with her household. The jailer, the same night, with all his. Timothy comes to faith through his mother and grandmother.

Public preaching absolutely happened, and it drew crowds. But the crowds were the front door. The households were the building.

Sociologists of religion studying this period keep landing on the same conclusion: new religious movements spread primarily through pre-existing social networks. People convert when someone they already trust converts first. That is not cynicism about the Spirit — it is a description of the ordinary means the Spirit tends to use.

#### They were unusually good at the unglamorous parts

The early Christians developed a reputation for behaviour that made no economic sense. They cared for their sick instead of fleeing plague cities. They buried the poor. They took in abandoned infants. They fed widows who were not their relatives.

Even hostile observers noted it. The emperor Julian, trying to revive Roman paganism, complained bitterly that the Christians had won influence through their care of strangers and the poor, and urged his own priests to copy it.

This is worth sitting with. The most effective apologetic of the early Church was not a superior argument. It was a visible, costly, sustained pattern of love that the surrounding culture could not account for.

#### Multiplication, not addition

Here is the part that most changes how you read your own map. Every person in a household network has a household network of their own.

When one person begins following Jesus, they carry the Gospel into rooms you will never enter, among people who would never listen to you, as a trusted insider. That is why Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he has learned to reliable people *who will also teach others* — four generations deep in a single sentence.

Addition is reaching people yourself. Multiplication is helping a few people become the kind of people who reach their own world. One is limited by your capacity. The other is not.

On an [Oikos Map](https://www.oikosmap.com/#builder), this is the difference between a list of names and a branching diagram. Add a branch to someone and write in the people *they* know. The shape of the thing changes.

#### What this means for you, concretely

- **Your relationships are the strategy,** not a warm-up to it.
- **Your home is a legitimate venue.** A meal is a valid ministry.
- **Depth beats reach.** A few people you actually disciple will outperform a large audience you merely inform.
- **Consistency is the differentiator.** The early Church won on decades, not campaigns.
- **Aim for the fourth generation.** Ask the people you disciple who is in *their* oikos.

#### The scale, and your part in it

This is still unfinished. Around 2.3 billion people have little or no access to the Gospel, and roughly 4,490 people groups are considered unreached. You can see the current picture on [Love on Mission](https://www.loveonmission.world), which maps the Great Commission as it stands today.

Numbers that size can make a person feel pointless. Scripture is unusually direct about this: one plants, another waters, God makes it grow, and the planter and the waterer are simply co-workers with one purpose. No single person is the whole thing, and no faithful part is wasted.

Your part may be five names and five minutes a day. Historically, that is exactly what this has always been made of. If you want the wider vision, [Thy Kingdom Network](https://www.thykingdom.net) is the family these tools come from, and [Seek First World](https://www.seekfirst.world) presses the same question into work, art, and public life.

> I planted the seed, Apollos watered it, but God has been making it grow… The one who plants and the one who waters have one purpose… For we are co-workers in God's service. (1 Corinthians 3:6–9, NIV)

---

### Faith at Work: Your Coworkers Are Your Oikos
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/faith-at-work-your-coworkers-are-your-oikos · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-07-30

Most of us will spend something like 90,000 hours at work. For many, colleagues are the people we see most, after immediate family — and often we see them at their most stressed, most honest, and most human.

And yet work is the part of the oikos we are least equipped for. Church teaching tends to address family and neighbours. Work gets a talk about integrity and little else.

#### Competence is part of the witness

Start here, because it is the part most often skipped. Doing your job well is not separate from being a faithful Christian at work — it is the foundation of it.

Nobody is persuaded about eternity by someone who misses deadlines and talks about grace. Being reliable, prepared, honest about mistakes, and genuinely good at your work buys you something no evangelism strategy can: credibility.

Colossians tells slaves — people with far less agency than any of us — to work as though working for the Lord. If that applied there, it certainly applies to a spreadsheet.

This is also where the practical matters. Faithfulness is largely logistics: if the follow-up you promised never got scheduled, it never happened. Tools like [TaskSimply](https://tasksimply.com) exist for exactly that unglamorous problem.

#### What actually gets noticed

In a workplace, these are the things people register over months:

- **How you speak about absent colleagues.** Refusing to join a pile-on is loud.
- **How you handle being wrong.** Owning it fully, without spin, is genuinely rare.
- **How you treat people with nothing to offer you.** Cleaners, juniors, contractors, the difficult client.
- **Whether you are the same person under pressure.** Character shows up at quarter-end.
- **Whether you protect your rest.** A Christian who is not frantic is a quiet argument that their identity rests somewhere other than performance.

#### How faith comes up naturally

You rarely need to engineer this. Work generates the questions on its own: a redundancy round, a diagnosis, a divorce, a birth, a colleague quietly falling apart in a meeting room.

What you need is to be the kind of person who is safe to talk to when it happens, and honest enough not to hide where your own hope comes from. "I was praying about that on the way in" is a normal sentence, said normally.

Two things to avoid. Do not use your position to pressure people who report to you — that is an abuse of power, however well intended. And do not perform. Sincerity survives scrutiny; a persona does not.

#### If you lead or own the business

Authority changes the calculus. You cannot evangelise downward without the power dynamic doing the talking. But you can shape something more far-reaching: how the organisation treats people.

Wages that are actually fair. Hours that do not quietly consume families. Honesty with customers when it costs you. Space for people to be human. These decisions preach to everyone who works there, and they are available only to you.

[Lions Den Alliance](https://www.lionsdenalliance.com) is a network of business owners refusing to split faith from work in exactly this way, and [Seek First World](https://www.seekfirst.world) presses the same question across culture more broadly — work, media, art, and civic life.

#### Keeping track without being strange about it

Colleagues belong on your [Oikos Map](https://www.oikosmap.com/#builder) alongside family and neighbours. Put them there. Note what they mentioned. Pray for them by name.

If you are working with a team, or your list has grown past what one page can hold, [Kingdom Base](https://kingdombase.app) is built for tracking conversations and follow-ups properly across a group.

And guard the source. Sustained witness in a demanding job runs on something, and if that something is willpower it will not last. [I Am Reborn](https://www.iamreborn.net) is about that formation — spirit, mind, body, purpose — and [Daniel Ziedins](https://www.danielziedins.com) writes on faith, work, and building things that serve the Kingdom.

> Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters. (Colossians 3:23, NIV)

---

### How to Invite Someone to Church Without It Being Awkward
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-invite-someone-to-church · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-08-13

Ask people how they first ended up in a church, and you will hear the same answer over and over: **someone invited them.** Not a campaign, not an algorithm — a person they already knew, who asked.

And yet inviting someone is the step most of us quietly avoid. Not because we lack conviction, but because we are afraid of the ten seconds of awkwardness between asking and hearing the answer.

#### Why it feels awkward (and why it usually is not)

The fear is that inviting someone changes the relationship — that you stop being a friend and become a project. It is a fair fear, and it is worth naming, because it is exactly what people can sense.

But notice what is actually happening in your head. You are rehearsing a rejection that has not occurred, on behalf of a person who has not been asked. Most people, when invited warmly to something that matters to a friend, are not offended. They are mildly flattered, even when they say no.

The invitation is not the hard part. Deciding to risk the small, brief awkwardness is the hard part.

#### Start lower than a Sunday service

A Sunday morning service is a surprisingly high-commitment ask. It involves unfamiliar customs, standing and sitting on cue, songs everyone else knows, and no obvious exit. For someone with no church background, it can feel like walking into a private members club mid-conversation.

There is usually a lower rung on the ladder, and lower rungs get climbed more often:

- **Your table.** A meal at your home asks almost nothing of them and shows almost everything about you.
- **Something joyful and public.** A free outdoor event is far easier to accept than a service — nobody has to know the etiquette.
- **A practical thing.** Serving together at a food drive or a community day. Doing beats watching.
- **A conversation with a set end.** A course or discussion group with a fixed number of weeks removes the fear of open-ended commitment.
- **Then a service** — once they know at least one other face in the room.

This is why an event like [Jesus Festival](https://www.jesusfestival.ca) is such a useful first rung: it is free, outdoors, family-friendly, and requires no religious literacy to enjoy. The [movement behind it](https://www.jesusfestivalmovement.com) exists precisely so that whole cities get an easy front door.

#### How to word it

Three things make an invitation land: be specific, be casual, and give them a graceful way out.

**Specific.** "You should come sometime" is not an invitation — it is a sentiment. "There is a thing on Saturday at two, I am going, would you like to come with me?" is an invitation.

**Casual.** Say it the way you would invite someone to a barbecue, because the weight in your voice tells them how big a deal you think this is. If you sound nervous, they will assume there is something to be nervous about.

**Escapable.** Add the line that removes the pressure: *"No stress at all if it is not your thing."* Counter-intuitively, people say yes more often when it is genuinely easy to say no.

And go with them. "Come to my church" is a much bigger ask than "come with me." Offer the lift, meet them outside, sit with them, and plan what happens afterwards so they are not left standing alone in a room of strangers.

#### When they say no

Say "no problem at all" and mean it. Then — and this is the part that matters — treat them exactly the same next week.

If your warmth dips after a no, you have told them the friendship was conditional, and they will remember that far longer than the invitation. If nothing changes, you have told them something truer than any sermon: that you actually just like them.

A no is also rarely permanent. It often means "not this week", "not that kind of thing", or "I am not ready to be seen doing that yet." Ask again in a few months, about something different.

#### Who to ask first

Look at your [Oikos Map](https://www.oikosmap.com/#builder) and find the people already at the **Care** stage — the ones you have been praying for and have moved toward practically. Those relationships have enough trust in them to carry an invitation.

Pick one. Choose the specific thing you will invite them to, and the day you will ask. Vague intentions do not survive a busy week; [put it in whatever you actually use to plan](https://tasksimply.com), the way you would any other commitment.

If your church does not currently have an obvious low-rung thing to invite people to, that is worth solving. [Love on The World](https://www.loveontheworld.com) helps groups create exactly that, and [Love on Hamilton](https://www.loveonhamilton.com) is a working example of a city where the invitations are easy to make.

> "Nazareth! Can anything good come from there?" Nathanael asked. "Come and see," said Philip. (John 1:46, NIV)

---

### What to Actually Say When Someone Is Going Through Something Hard
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/what-to-say-when-someone-is-hurting · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-08-13

Someone on your map is about to go through something hard. A diagnosis, a redundancy, a marriage coming apart, a funeral. And when it happens, most of us go quiet — not because we do not care, but because we are terrified of saying the wrong thing.

So here is the thing worth knowing before it happens: **saying nothing is the one option guaranteed to hurt.** Almost everything else can be repaired.

#### What people actually remember

Ask anyone who has been through grief what helped, and they rarely recall a sentence. They recall who turned up. The friend who sat with them. The neighbour who mowed the lawn without asking. The colleague who kept texting after everyone else stopped.

They also remember who vanished. Usually those people were not unkind — they were waiting until they knew what to say, and the moment passed.

This should be freeing. You are not being assessed on eloquence. You are being asked to be present.

#### Sentences that help

When you genuinely do not know what to say, say one of these. They are short on purpose.

- **"I am so sorry. I do not have words."** Honest, and better than a borrowed platitude.
- **"You do not have to talk. I just wanted to sit with you."**
- **"I am bringing dinner Thursday. Do you prefer chicken or pasta?"** A decision, not an offer.
- **"Tell me about them."** To the bereaved, this is a gift. People are often desperate to say the name out loud.
- **"I have been praying for you this week."** Said plainly, almost never unwelcome.
- **"I am still here."** Sent in week six, when everyone else has moved on. This one carries the most weight of all.

#### Sentences that hurt, however well meant

Most of these come from a good place. They land badly because they are trying to resolve the pain rather than share it.

- **"Everything happens for a reason."** Asks them to justify their loss while they are still inside it.
- **"God needed another angel."** Not true, and it makes God the author of their worst day.
- **"At least..."** Nothing good has ever followed those two words in this context.
- **"Let me know if you need anything."** Kindly meant, but it hands the work to the person with the least capacity to do it.
- **"I know exactly how you feel."** You do not, and it quietly turns the conversation toward you.
- **Rushing to a verse.** Scripture is deeply comforting later. Deployed too early it can feel like being told to stop crying.

If you get one of these wrong — and you will — do not spiral about it. "I said that badly last week, I am sorry" repairs almost anything. Withdrawing out of embarrassment does far more damage than the original clumsiness.

#### Be specific, and be there in six weeks

Crisis attracts a crowd for about a fortnight. Then the casseroles stop, the messages thin out, and the person is left alone with a life that has permanently changed. **The most valuable thing you can do is be the person who shows up in week six.**

Put it in your calendar now — a reminder to check in a month from today. That is not cold or mechanical; it is the only reliable way to beat the natural fade of attention.

And be concrete. Do the specific thing: the lift to the appointment, the school run, the paperwork nobody has energy for. When care is organised rather than improvised it reaches further, which is the whole idea behind [Kingdom Response](https://www.kingdomresponse.com) — churches showing up practically when disaster hits — and [Love on Hamilton](https://www.loveonhamilton.com) at a city scale.

#### On praying with them

Ask first: *"Would it be alright if I prayed for you?"* Almost everyone says yes, including people with no faith at all. And if they say no, respect it instantly and warmly — that is its own act of love.

Keep it short and plain. Name what is actually happening rather than smoothing it over. You are not performing; you are carrying someone to God who has not the strength to walk there themselves.

Then keep praying for them by name afterwards. On your [Oikos Map](https://www.oikosmap.com/#builder), put what they are facing in the notes beside their name so you remember to ask about the specific thing next time. Remembering the details is love made visible — and [Daniel and Katie](https://www.kd-ziedins.com) write about learning this in the middle of everyday family life.

> Rejoice with those who rejoice; mourn with those who mourn. (Romans 12:15, NIV)

---

### How to Disciple Someone When You Do Not Feel Qualified
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/how-to-disciple-someone · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-09-24

Someone asks you a real question about faith, or starts coming to church, or actually wants to read the Bible with you. And the first thing most of us feel is not joy. It is panic: *I am not qualified for this.*

Almost everyone who has ever discipled anyone felt that at the time. It is not a disqualification. It is the normal starting condition.

#### The bar is lower than you think

Discipling someone does not mean having answers to everything. It means being about a step ahead, walking in the same direction, and being honest about the parts you are still working out.

Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he has heard to reliable people who will teach others. Note what is being passed on: not credentials, not expertise — **what you have received**. You can only give what you have, and what you have is enough to start.

In practice the qualification is character, not knowledge. Are you actually following Jesus? Will you show up consistently? Will you admit when you do not know? That is the list.

#### A pattern you can repeat

You do not need a curriculum. You need a rhythm simple enough that you will still be doing it in six months. This one works for a coffee shop, a lunch break, or a phone call:

- **Catch up honestly.** Ten minutes. How is life actually going? Do not skip this to get to the "real" content — this is where trust is built.
- **Read a short passage together.** Out loud. A few paragraphs, not a chapter. A Gospel is the right place to start.
- **Ask: what stands out?** Let them answer first. Resist the urge to teach. Their own observation will stick a hundred times harder than your explanation.
- **Ask: what will you do about it?** This is the question that turns a Bible study into discipleship. Something small and specific, this week.
- **Ask: who could you tell?** Not pressure — just the habit of passing it on from the very beginning.
- **Pray for each other.** Both directions. Being prayed for by the person you are discipling changes the relationship for the better.

That is the whole thing. Forty minutes. If you did only that, every fortnight, for a year, you would have done something most people never receive.

#### What to do when you do not know

They will ask something you cannot answer. Suffering, hell, a hard passage, why the Church has behaved badly.

Say so. *"I do not know. Let us find out."* Then actually find out — ask your pastor, read something solid, come back the next time with what you learned.

Two things happen when you do this. They get the answer, and they learn what an honest follower of Jesus does with a hard question. The second lesson outlasts the first.

What you must not do is bluff. People can tell, and a bluff quietly teaches them that faith requires pretending.

#### Boundaries that keep it healthy

- **Disciple your own sex,** particularly one to one. This protects everyone and removes a whole category of complication.
- **You are not their counsellor.** If something serious surfaces — abuse, addiction, self-harm — care for them and help them to a professional. Discipleship is not therapy.
- **You are not their saviour.** You cannot make anyone grow. One plants, another waters, God gives the growth.
- **Let it end well.** Not every pairing lasts forever. A season that ends cleanly is a success, not a failure.

#### Aim past the person in front of you

Here is the shift that changes everything: you are not discipling someone so that they become a well-taught Christian. You are discipling them so that they can do this for someone else.

So say that out loud, early. *"At some point you are going to do this with someone, and that is the point."* It reframes everything they learn — they start listening as someone who will pass it on, not just someone receiving.

Then ask the question this whole site is built around: *who is in your oikos?* Help them make their own [Oikos Map](https://www.oikosmap.com/#builder). The moment they start praying for their own five names, the thing has multiplied beyond you.

If you are doing this with more than a couple of people, keeping track gets hard — [Kingdom Base](https://kingdombase.app) is built for exactly that, and [Love on The World](https://www.loveontheworld.com) helps a whole group start together rather than alone.

> And the things you have heard me say in the presence of many witnesses entrust to reliable people who will also be qualified to teach others. (2 Timothy 2:2, NIV)

---

### How to Pray for Your City (Without It Feeling Abstract)
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/praying-for-your-city · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-09-24

Praying for your city can feel like praying for the weather — enormous, vague, and impossible to tell whether anything happened.

But a city is not an abstraction. It is a number of streets, and on each of them people are having the hardest week of their lives. Here is how to pray for a place in a way that stays concrete enough to keep doing.

#### Start with the ground you actually touch

Your [Oikos Map](https://www.oikosmap.com/#builder) is the first circle. Your street is the second. Before praying for a whole city, pray for the part of it you can see from your front door.

Walk it, if you can. Not a march, not anything anyone would notice — just a walk, praying quietly for the houses you pass. It is remarkable how differently you see a street you have prayed down.

You will start noticing things: the house that is always dark, the neighbour whose car has not moved, the family that arrived last month. Prayer turns scenery into people.

#### Pray for the places, not just the population

A city runs on institutions, and each is full of people under real pressure:

- **Schools** — teachers who are exhausted, kids carrying things nobody knows about.
- **Hospitals** — staff making decisions on no sleep, families in the worst hour of their lives.
- **Emergency services** — people who see what the rest of us are spared.
- **Local government** — whether you like them or not; Scripture is direct about praying for those in authority.
- **Businesses** — owners deciding whether they can keep staff on.
- **Churches** — all of them, not only yours. A city is not reached by one congregation.

Pick one a day and you have a week. That is a sustainable rhythm, and it is far more concrete than "Lord, bless our city."

#### Pray for peace, and then be part of the answer

Jeremiah tells exiles to seek the peace and prosperity of the city they did not choose, and to pray for it — *because if it prospers, you prosper*. Their wellbeing and the city's were tied together.

That has a sharp edge. Praying for a city you refuse to be inconvenienced by is not really prayer; it is commentary. The prayer and the presence belong together.

So let the prayer produce something. Learn the name of someone at the shop. Show up to the community thing. Give to the food bank you have been praying about. [Love on Hamilton](https://www.loveonhamilton.com) is what this looks like when churches do it together on purpose, and [Kingdom Response](https://www.kingdomresponse.com) is the same instinct when crisis hits.

#### Do it with other people

City-sized prayer is hard to sustain alone, and it was never meant to be. Find two or three others. Walk together. Pray the same streets.

If you want something structured, [Love on The World](https://www.loveontheworld.com) exists to help a few friends start praying for and loving their city together, and the [Jesus Festival app](https://www.jesusfestival.app) has a live prayer wall where a whole community carries requests between them.

And keep the long view. Cities do not change on a quarterly timeline. One plants, another waters, God gives the growth — and some of the answers will be gathered in by people who come after you.

> Seek the peace and prosperity of the city to which I have carried you… Pray to the Lord for it, because if it prospers, you too will prosper. (Jeremiah 29:7, NIV)

---

### Plunder Hell, Populate Heaven: Your Part in Sending the Gospel
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/plunder-hell-populate-heaven · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-10-05

Somewhere tonight, a man will lie awake in a city you have never visited, wondering whether anyone is out there. He has never heard the name of Jesus said with love. Nobody in his oikos knows it to tell him.

Your Oikos Map is about the people within reach of you. This article is about the people who are not — and the remarkable truth that you can still play a real part in reaching them.

#### The war is real, and so is the rescue

Scripture does not describe evangelism as a marketing exercise. It describes a rescue. God *"has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of the Son he loves"* (Colossians 1:13). Every person who comes to faith is someone carried out of one kingdom and into another.

Jesus put it in even sharper terms. Explaining how He drove out darkness, He asked how anyone could enter a strong man's house and carry off his possessions *"unless he first ties up the strong man? Then he can plunder his house"* (Matthew 12:29). Christ has already bound the strong man. The Church is sent in after Him to bring people home.

That is where the phrase **"plunder hell and populate heaven"** comes from — the motto the evangelist Reinhard Bonnke carried around the world. It is not bravado. It is simply what the Great Commission is: taking back what was never the enemy's to keep, and filling heaven with people Jesus died for. And Jesus promised the gates of Hades would not hold out against it (Matthew 16:18).

#### Nobody does this alone — and nobody is left out

Here is the part most of us miss. The New Testament never imagines a mission carried by heroes while everyone else watches. It imagines a body, where every part is necessary, and it names at least three ways to stand in the fight:

- **Go.** The people on your own Oikos Map are your front line. You are already sent to them.
- **Pray.** Jesus told us to ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers (Luke 10:2). Prayer is not the consolation prize for people who cannot go — it is front-line work.
- **Send.** Paul asked the obvious question: *"How can anyone preach unless they are sent?"* (Romans 10:15). Someone has to make it possible for those who go to keep going.

The apostle John goes further. Writing to a believer who looked after travelling missionaries, he urges him to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God (3 John 1:6), and explains why: *"We ought therefore to show hospitality to such people so that we may work together for the truth"* (3 John 1:8). The one who sends is not a spectator. They are a **co-worker** in the very same work.

#### The reward is shared

Paul wrote to the church in Philippi to thank them for their *"partnership in the gospel from the first day until now"* (Philippians 1:5). They had sent him support again and again. And he told them something astonishing about it: he did not desire their gifts; what he desired was *"that more be credited to your account"* (Philippians 4:17).

In other words, when the Philippians gave, the fruit of Paul's ministry was counted to them too. Every person who came to faith through his preaching was, in God's accounting, partly theirs.

That is still true. When you help send someone, the salvations, the baptisms and the churches planted through their work are not only their story. They are yours.

#### A ministry you can stand alongside

This tool exists because of Daniel and Katie Ziedins, and their story is a living picture of everything above.

As they tell it on [KD-Ziedins.com](https://www.kd-ziedins.com), it began in 2014 with [Love on Hamilton](https://www.loveonhamilton.com): weekly street evangelism and practical care for their city's homeless community. More than twelve years on, they describe salvations, healings, chains of addiction broken, and baptisms as regular testimonies — and a small outreach that grew into a weekly movement and then into [Love on The World](https://www.loveontheworld.com), taking the same work to other cities.

In 2022 they launched Overflow, a Sunday evening service where, in their words, the Holy Spirit was given full permission to move. They now serve with **e3 Canada**, which they describe as dedicated to equipping believers to evangelise and establish multiplying, life-changing churches. And each year they help gather their city at [Jesus Festival](https://www.jesusfestival.ca) in Hamilton — most recently this September at Gage Park.

Their current call is bold: **to help establish 100 multiplying outreach groups around the world** — ordinary believers, equipped and sent to bring the Gospel and practical love into their own communities. It is the Oikos Map vision, multiplied across nations.

#### How to stand with them

If something in you is stirring as you read this, here is what that can look like in practice:

- **Pray for them by name.** Put Daniel and Katie on your own Oikos Map, and pray for the 100 outreach groups to be raised up.
- **Partner financially.** Their ministry is supported through e3 Canada. You can give once or monthly at [their e3 Canada staff page](https://e3ministry.ca/staff/katie-daniel-ziedins).
- **Follow the story.** [KD-Ziedins.com](https://www.kd-ziedins.com) carries their ministry updates, evangelism training and what God is doing — so your prayers can be specific.
- **Start a group where you are.** If you want to be one of the hundred, [Love on The World](https://www.loveontheworld.com) exists to help a few friends start reaching their city together.
- **Pass it on.** Send this to one person who has a heart for the nations.

Monthly partnership matters most, because it lets a ministry plan rather than survive. But no gift is too small, and no prayer is wasted.

#### Your part is not small

One day the full harvest will be gathered in. People from every nation, tribe and language will stand before the throne (Revelation 7:9). Some of them will be there because someone went. Some, because someone prayed. Some, because someone sent.

One plants, another waters, God gives the growth — and the planter and the waterer, Paul says, *"have one purpose"* (1 Corinthians 3:8). Plunder hell. Populate heaven. You have a place in it, starting today.

> How, then, can they call on the one they have not believed in? And how can they believe in the one of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone preaching to them? And how can anyone preach unless they are sent? (Romans 10:14–15, NIV)

---

### From Hamilton's Streets to the Nations: What 12 Years of Saying Yes Has Built
https://www.oikosmap.com/blog/from-hamilton-to-the-nations · Daniel Ziedins · 2026-10-06

In 2014, a handful of believers walked onto the streets of Hamilton, Ontario with food, coffee and the name of Jesus. Nobody wrote a press release. It was one night, on one street, in one city.

Twelve years later, that same yes has become weekly outreach in twelve cities, a city-wide festival, a training partnership with e3 Canada, and a brand being built to carry the Kingdom into culture. This is that story — and an invitation to be part of the next chapter.

#### Do not despise the day of small things

When the people of Israel stood over a half-built temple feeling foolish, God asked them a question that has encouraged every small beginning since: *"Who dares despise the day of small things?"* (Zechariah 4:10).

Love on Hamilton was a small thing. As Daniel and Katie Ziedins tell it on [KD-Ziedins.com](https://www.kd-ziedins.com), it began in 2014 as weekly street evangelism and practical care for the city's homeless community — sharing the Gospel with everyone they met. They describe salvations, healings, chains of addiction broken and baptisms becoming regular testimonies on those streets.

Jesus said the Kingdom is like a mustard seed — *"the smallest of all seeds, yet when it grows, it is the largest of garden plants"* (Matthew 13:32). That is not a metaphor about ambition. It is a promise about what God does with faithfulness.

#### From one city to twelve: Love on The World

Jesus gave His followers a pattern for expansion: *"you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth"* (Acts 1:8). Start where you are. Then keep going.

That is exactly what happened next. The Hamilton outreach grew into [Love on The World](https://www.loveontheworld.com) — a movement that, by its own description, helps ordinary believers share the Gospel, meet practical needs, make disciples and multiply weekly outreach groups. Today it reports groups meeting **weekly in 12 cities** for street outreach, prayer and practical compassion.

The part worth noticing is who leads them. Not professionals — ordinary believers. Love on The World says newcomers need no experience beforehand, and that anyone can begin a "Love on [City]" outreach where they live. Its evangelism field guide, prayer-walk builder, seven-day new-believer journey and prayer points for the nations are free and need no account.

This is the Oikos Map idea at city scale: the people God has placed around you, reached by people who simply decided to go.

#### A city gathered around one name: Jesus Festival

Some things are too big for a street corner. Each year [Jesus Festival](https://www.jesusfestival.ca) gathers Hamilton at Gage Park for a free, family-friendly weekend of worship, testimonies, prayer and practical love — no ticket required.

Jesus Festival 2026 took place on September 4–5 and, in the festival's own words, drew a record turnout. **Early reports** it has shared include **70+ people giving their lives to Jesus**, **50+ baptisms**, more than **3,000 free hot dogs and drinks** served, and many healings and deliverances, with altar calls on both Friday and Saturday. 2026 was also the first Jesus Festival Niagara, where the city lit Niagara Falls yellow in recognition of it.

Numbers are not the point — every one of those seventy is a name, a family, an oikos. But they are a glimpse of what Jesus meant when He said the harvest is plentiful (Matthew 9:37).

#### Equipping the Church: e3 Canada

A festival is a moment. Lasting fruit needs churches and disciple-makers who keep going on Monday.

That is why Daniel and Katie serve with **e3 Canada**, which they describe as equipping believers to evangelise and establish multiplying, life-changing churches. Alongside it, they launched Overflow in 2022 — a Sunday evening gathering where, in their words, the Holy Spirit was given full permission to move.

Their current call is the most ambitious yet: **to help establish 100 multiplying outreach groups around the world** — ordinary believers, equipped and sent to bring the Gospel and practical love into their own communities.

#### Into culture: SIX33

Jesus did not call His people to hide in a corner. *"You are the light of the world. A town built on a hill cannot be hidden"* (Matthew 5:14). Culture is part of everyone's oikos — the clothes, the stories, the athletes and the creators people look to.
